questions.question_text:
The table shows the distribution of $X$, the number of cars parked in a randomly chosen driveway.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.18 & 0.44 & 0.3 & 0.08 \end{array}$
Find $P(X=2)$.

options.why: Counted the columns starting at $x=1$, so read the entry above $x=3$.
Treated the first column as $x=1$, so read the entry above $x=1$.
Added $P(2)$ and $P(3)$ instead of reading a single probability.

questions.solution_text:
$P(X=2)$ is the entry in the column headed $x=2$.
$P(X=2)=0.3$

questions.question_text:
A discrete random variable $X$ has this distribution.
$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.1 & 0.25 & 0.3 & 0.2 & 0.15 \end{array}$
Find $P(3 \le X < 6)$.

options.why: Included $x=6$, although the strict inequality $X<6$ excludes it.
Excluded $x=3$, reading $3 \le X$ as a strict inequality.
Excluded $x=3$ and included $x=6$, reversing both endpoint conventions.

questions.solution_text:
The values included are $3$, $4$ and $5$.
$P(3 \le X < 6)=0.25+0.3+0.2$
$=0.75$

questions.question_text:
The distribution of $X$ is given below, where $c$ is a constant.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 3c & 5c & 4c & 8c \end{array}$
Find $c$.

options.why: Divided $1$ by the number of outcomes, as though the distribution were uniform.
Solved $20c=1$ by multiplying instead of dividing.
Added the coefficients $3+5+4+8$ as $19$.

questions.question_text:
Is the table below a probability distribution?
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.4 & 0.35 & -0.05 & 0.3 \end{array}$

options.text: No, because $P(X=3)$ is negative and a probability cannot be less than $0$.
Yes, because the four probabilities add to $1$.
options.why: Checked only the total and ignored the requirement that every probability lies between $0$ and $1$.

options.text: No, because the probabilities add to $1.1$ rather than $1$.
options.why: Added $0.05$ instead of subtracting it, so the total was computed incorrectly.

options.text: No, because the four probabilities are not all equal.
options.why: Applied the uniform condition instead of the general conditions for a distribution.

questions.solution_text:
$0.4+0.35-0.05+0.3=1$, so the total is correct.
However $P(X=3)=-0.05$, which is negative.
A probability cannot be negative, so this is not a probability distribution.

questions.question_text:
A box holds $2$ lemons and $5$ limes.
Two pieces of fruit are taken at random without replacement.
Let $X$ be the number of lemons taken.
Find $P(X=1)$.

options.why: Counted only lemon-then-lime and missed the lime-then-lemon order.
Used with-replacement probabilities, keeping $7$ items for the second draw.
Found $P(X=2)$, the probability that both are lemons, instead.

questions.question_text:
A function is given by $P(x)=\frac{x^{2}}{k}$ for $x \in \{1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4\}$.
Find the value of $k$ that makes this a probability distribution.

options.why: Added the values $1+2+3+4$ without squaring them first.
Squared the total $1+2+3+4$ instead of adding the individual squares.
Used the number of values, as though each probability were $\frac{1}{4}$.
Included the bar above $x=1$, reading $X \ge 2$ as $X \ge 1$.
Read only the last bar, treating $X \ge 2$ as the largest value alone.
Read only the bar above $x=2$, ignoring the values beyond it.

questions.solution_text:
The bar above $x=2$ has height $0.3$ and the bar above $x=3$ has height $0.2$.
$P(X \ge 2)=0.3+0.2$
$=0.5$

questions.question_text:
Let $N$ be the number of times a household recycling bin is emptied in a month, and suppose $P(N \ge 2)=0.86$.
Which statement says what this means?

options.text: The probability that the bin is emptied at least twice in a month is $0.86$.
The probability that the bin is emptied more than twice in a month is $0.86$.
options.why: Read $\ge$ as strictly greater than, dropping the value $2$ itself.

options.text: The probability that the bin is emptied exactly twice in a month is $0.86$.
options.why: Read the statement as $P(N=2)$ rather than as a cumulative probability.

options.text: The probability that the bin is emptied at most twice in a month is $0.86$.
options.why: Read $\ge$ as $\le$, reversing the inequality.

questions.solution_text:
$N \ge 2$ means $N$ takes the value $2$ or any value above it.
The probability that the bin is emptied at least twice in a month is $0.86$.

questions.question_text:
A spinner has $4$ equal sectors, exactly one of which is shaded.
The spinner is spun $3$ times.
Let $X$ be the number of spins that land on the shaded sector.
Find $P(X \ge 1)$.

options.why: Found $P(X=0)$ and stopped, without subtracting it from $1$.
Used only $2$ spins, giving $1-\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^{2}$ instead of $1-\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^{3}$.
Added $\frac{1}{4}$ once per spin, treating the three spins as though they could not overlap.

questions.solution_text:
Each spin lands on the shaded sector with probability $\frac{1}{4}$, and the spins are independent.
$P(X \ge 1)=1-P(X=0)$
$P(X=0)=\frac{3}{4} \times \frac{3}{4} \times \frac{3}{4}$
$=\frac{27}{64}$
$P(X \ge 1)=1-\frac{27}{64}$
$=\frac{37}{64}$

questions.question_text:
The probability distribution is modelled by $P(X=r)=k(r+1)$ for $r=1,2,3$, and $P(X=r)=0$ otherwise.
What is the value of $k$?

options.why: Uses an incorrect total for the three probability weights.
Gives the normalisation sum rather than solving for the constant.
The probabilities can be summed directly to determine the constant.

questions.solution_text: The probabilities must sum to one: $k(2+3+4)=9k=1$. Therefore $k=\dfrac19$.
